title: Transparent staged-free backpressure and page holdovers in variable-length continuous batching
creator: Marco Chen
description:
Summary: Production inference fleet shows slow, reproducible resident GPU memory growth under mixed-length continuous batching. Behavior looks like a leak (RSS climbs across hours) but investigation indicates deferred-free backlog, cross-stream free ordering, and pinned staging pages being held alive across pool boundaries. This ticket captures the investigation, reproducer, telemetry to add, mitigation experiments, and a proposal for a short-term patch and longer-term allocator changes.

Observed symptoms:
- Gradual GPU resident memory increase over 6–12 hours when serving workloads with mixed short (<=64) and long (>=1024) tokens in the same runtime.
- Frequent small-spike latency regressions during batch merges coincident with allocation churn.
- cudaMallocAsync deferred free queue depth (observed via our custom allocator metrics) climbs to 1000s, correlated with pinned staging bytes not being released to OS.
- GPU mem snapshots show many small device-owned extents marked as free in pool metadata but still resident on device.
- Reproduces reliably on dedicated M60-equivalent pools and on our A100 testbed when using real traffic replay with sequence-length mixing.

Reproducer (short):
1) Run workload-replay-pipeline with mixed_trace_v3.json (attached to Drive) that interleaves 90% short/10% long requests in continuous batching mode.
2) Start allocator telemetry script (alloc-trace.sh) which records deferred_free_depth, pool_resident_bytes, staging_pinned_bytes, and per-stream pending_free_count every 10s.
3) Observe resident growth after ~30–90 minutes and deferred_free_depth ramping.

Investigation notes and findings:
- Hypothesis 1: cudaMallocAsync deferred free batches are not draining because frees are posted to streams that are not synchronized due to our continuous merging strategy. When long requests hold a stream's work, frees accumulate behind them.
- Hypothesis 2: The staging/pinned host buffer used for device->host transfers is being recycled into the allocator's pinned pool without a final cudaFreeAsync drain; the pool keeps the pages pinned and they remain resident until the device driver reconciles them, which our code path never triggers frequently.
- Hypothesis 3: Pool compaction thresholds are too conservative for fragmented patterns produced by interleaved short/long sequences; small free extents scattered across arenas are not coalesced and therefore not returned to the OS.
- Correlation: deferred_free_depth and staging_pinned_bytes are the strongest predictors of RSS climb in regression tests (Pearson r ~0.78).

Short-term mitigations attempted (results):
- Periodic cudaDeviceSynchronize() in the batch merge path (experiment A): forced drain reduces backlog but adds 2–6ms median latency and is unacceptable at scale.
- Introduced a background epoch trim thread that calls a limited cudaDeviceSynchronize on a low-priority stream every 30s (experiment B): reduced resident growth significantly in test but added nondeterministic jitter and occasional 200ms spikes in tail latency.
- Lowered deferred-free batching window from 512 -> 64 frees (experiment C): lowered memory growth and minimal latency impact. This is promising but increases kernel invocation overhead in very busy cases.

Proposed roadmap and changes: short-term (canary in runtime-1.20):
1) Add a ceiling on deferred_free_depth per-device-per-pool (configurable, default 256). When ceiling reached, prefer opportunistic draining of oldest free batches on a dedicated low-priority internal stream.
2) Emit new telemetry metrics: deferred_free_depth, avg_free_batch_latency_ms, staging_pinned_bytes, pool_fragmentation_ratio (free_extents / total_extents), per-stream-pending-free-count. Add Grafana panels and alert if deferred_free_depth > 500 for 10m.
3) Backfill pooling policy: when reclaimed total resident < threshold for X minutes, proactively coalesce small extents into larger extents and release to OS. Tunable to avoid frequent kernel churn.

Longer-term design proposals (runtime-1.22):
- Per-stream free credits: allow streams to post frees but hold credit-limited ownership so a long-running stream cannot fence infinite frees. Those credits are replenished when the stream makes progress.
- Cross-stream free re-assignment: if a free batch is blocked behind an active kernel for >T ms, migrate the free work to an internal maintenance stream with proper ordering semantics using cudaGraph-merged dependencies to avoid global sync.
- Better fragmentation-aware allocator: track adjacency and age for extents and prefer compaction when fragmentation increases during mixed-length traffic patterns.

Telemetry and dashboards added in this ticket:
- Grafana: fleet/runtime/memory/deferred_free_depth (per cluster/device pool)
- Alert: deferred_free_depth > 500 for 10m -> paging to #infra-oncall
- Canary dashboard: staging_pinned_bytes / pool_resident_bytes heatmap by model family

Testing plan:
- Stage canary on 5 dedicated instances in eu-west-1 with realistic replay trace for 72 hours.
- Run A/B with lowered deferred-free-batching window vs. default. Measure tail latency, per-token cost delta, and RSS differential.
- Run synthetic adversarial test (100% short then 100% long) to confirm no regressions in worst-case churn.

Artifacts and links:
- Reproducer trace: drive.redwood/app/drive/mixed_trace_v3.json (internal)
- Alloc telemetry script: github.com/redwood/infra/alloc-trace (PR #1256)
- Draft design doc: confluence.redwood/runtime/allocator/compact-and-deferred-free-design (internal)
- Canary PR: github.com/redwood/runtime/pull/3421 (allocator: enforce deferred-free ceiling)

Acceptance criteria for short-term patch:
- No fleet-wide increase in 95th latency > 5% during canary compared to baseline.
- Deferred_free_depth alarm triggers resolved within 30 minutes and resident growth plateaued for canary hosts.
- No reproducible OOMs introduced by compaction heuristics.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How to choose deferred_free_depth ceiling across a variety of GPU types (A100 vs older cards) without manual per-hardware tuning? Suggest adaptive ceiling based on recent free throughput metrics.
- Is periodic low-priority drain an acceptable operational burden if we can bound latency spikes? Might be necessary for heavy long-running kernels.
- How to test cross-stream free migration in CI reliably? Needs synthetic multi-stream harness and validation of ordering semantics.
